lesson.title: Jailbreaks and guardrails
lesson.subtitle: Why chatbots say no, how people try to talk them round, and what holds

video.title: Jailbreaks and guardrails

chapters.label: The lab, and what you can do

scenes.visual: Cards: A chatbot; “Just pretend”; Hurtful jokes.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In break, I heard two students boasting. One had made a chatbot write rude jokes about a teacher, just by telling it to pretend. They laughed, but the jokes were about a real person, and they hurt.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: why chatbots say no, how people try to talk them round, and the guardrails that hold.

scenes.visual: A list: Hurting someone; Cheating and scams; Private details; Learned, like a habit.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Chatbots are trained to refuse some requests: help to hurt someone, to cheat, to scam, or to find someone's private details. Those refusals are learned, like a habit. They work best for the wordings the chatbot was trained on.

scenes.visual: A list: Play a role; “Just for a story”; Split into innocent pieces; Switch language.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A jailbreak is an attempt to talk a chatbot past its rules. People ask it to play a role, say it's “just for a story”, split a request into innocent pieces, or switch language. They're hunting for a wording the training missed.

scenes.visual: A list: Still hurts real people; Can be dangerously wrong; Breaks rules, blocks accounts.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: But a jailbreak isn't clever. Rude jokes still hurt a real teacher, and tricked answers can be dangerously wrong. It also breaks the app's rules, and can get your account blocked.

scenes.visual: A flow: Filter in → The model → Filter out → Check in code.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So builders don't rely on the chatbot alone. They add guardrails: rules around the model. A filter on what goes in. A filter on what comes out. And checks in code on anything the app does, like sending a message.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A filter blocks any message with the word “password”. Someone rewords a scam without that word. What happens?

scenes.visual: A table of three messages through a filter that blocks the word “password”: the plain scam is blocked, the reworded scam passes, an innocent lesson about passwords is blocked.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: It gets past. A word filter only catches what's on its list, so a new wording walks by. And it can block innocent messages too, like a lesson about passwords.

scenes.visual: A code card: a word filter that sends the reworded scam (it prints “sent”) changes into a check on the action that holds it (it prints “held: nobody said yes”).
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: A check on the action holds
scenes.narration: What holds is a check on the action itself. Before an app sends a message, code asks: did you ask for this, and did you say yes? However it's worded, an unapproved message never goes out.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Three guardrails; Plain, then reworded; The filter misses; The code check holds.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: rules around the model
scenes.narration: In the app, put three guardrails around Darsi Tiny. Send a scam in plain words, then reworded, and watch the word filter miss it. Then switch on the check in code, and see it hold every time.

scenes.visual: A list: Stop; Don't share it; Report it in the app; Tell an adult.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: And if a chatbot gives you something harmful or upsetting? Stop, and don't share it. Take a screenshot, report it in the app, and tell an adult you trust.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A classmate dares you to trick the school chatbot into saying something nasty about another student. What do you do?

scenes.visual: The summary: Refusals are learned; Word lists miss rewording; Code checks on actions hold; Stop, report, tell. Takeaway: Breaking a chatbot's rules isn't clever: reporting a gap is.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Learned · Filters miss · Code holds · Report
scenes.narration: Say no: it would hurt a real person and break the rules. Remember: refusals are learned, so rewording can slip past. Word filters miss new wordings, but checks in code on actions hold. And when a chatbot goes wrong: stop, report, tell.

scenes.visual: A list: Find the report button; Before you need it; Three things you'd report; Share with a friend.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: find the report button in a chatbot or app you use, before you ever need it. Then write three things you'd report, and share the list with a friend.

checkpoints.prompt: A filter blocks any message containing the word “password”. Someone rewords a scam without that word. What happens?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: a word filter only catches what's on its list, so a new wording walks by.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the filter only knows its list of words. A reworded scam has none of them, so it passes.

checkpoints.prompt: A classmate dares you to trick the school chatbot into saying something nasty about another student. What do you do?

options.text: Try it: it's only a chatbot
Say no: it would hurt a real person and break the rules
Do it, but delete the chat afterwards

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: the words would hurt a real student, whoever typed them, and it breaks the rules.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a chatbot's words still hurt a real student, and deleting the chat doesn't undo it.
